script:
Good morning. Here's your briefing for Thursday, September 24.

First up, AI & Tech.

A new paper proposes a concept called "Infinite-Parameter LLMs." The architecture uses a hypernetwork to generate and adapt model weights from live data during interactions. This would allow the model to learn online without its weights being frozen after pre-training, representing new knowledge in the weights themselves rather than just in the context window.

On the developer tool front, a new YC startup has launched Skillsync, which aims to make AI chat sessions portable across different coding agents. It uses an open-source Rust engine called txcript—that’s T-X-C-R-I-P-T—to act as a universal converter for the entire session history, including messages, reasoning, and tool calls. The tool is a local-first desktop app that lets you move a session to a new agent without starting over.

And in a related practical note, a blog post suggests reframing how we use large language models for classification. Instead of using a model's direct output as the final verdict, it argues you should treat the LLM's prediction as a feature, which is then fed into a simpler, traditional classifier like logistic regression. This approach is proposed to solve common problems with calibration and threshold control.

In moves from the major labs, Anthropic is consolidating its Claude AI features into a single interface and has launched new document tools. Meanwhile, Meta’s Muse AI agent is now available as a Mac application. And OpenAI is expanding its advertising model with something called Sponsored Agents.

The Advanced AI Society has joined the Linux Foundation and is launching what it calls an open verification ecosystem, prompted by a focus on agent security.

A couple of headlines with minimal detail: Stanford Medicine reports that AI agents created from manuscripts can now communicate with each other to make new discoveries. And The Rundown AI states that a co-creator of ChatGPT has launched a new kind of AI, though no further details were provided.

Finally, OpenAI has announced a new disclosure system for AI behavior and in the process, revealed some past instances of use it deemed "concerning."

Next, US Headlines.

The White House has withdrawn its nominee to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, after a key Republican senator who had previously championed the pick suddenly objected to the nomination. The move leaves the agency, which has been without a Senate-confirmed director for years, in continued leadership uncertainty.

In Alabama, the state has executed an inmate convicted of a 1998 double murder, following a last-minute refusal by the Supreme Court to intervene. The execution by lethal injection went forward after a previous attempt to use nitrogen gas was blocked by the courts.

Meanwhile, a report from the Department of Homeland Security confirms that a Florida immigration facility nicknamed "Alligator Alcatraz" used small outdoor cages for detainees. This follows testimony from a former detainee who said he was held in a phone booth-sized cage for fifteen hours, in what facility officials reportedly called a "calming area."

Former President Trump is threatening to tear down the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C., escalating a legal and political fight over the future of the iconic performing arts venue. The statement comes as a lawsuit connected to the center calls for the resignation of its leadership.

And in foreign policy news, Former President Trump has weighed in on discussions about Canada potentially forming a closer alliance with the European Union. While Canadian officials are exploring the idea to diversify international partnerships, Trump dismissed it, suggesting Canada should be more aligned with the United States.

Turning to Immigration & Visas.

Starting September eighteenth, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services will change how it evaluates green card applicants under the public charge rule. The agency is returning to a standard used before 2019, where it will consider the totality of an applicant's circumstances, such as their age, health, and financial resources. This change primarily affects those applying for adjustment of status from within the U.S. Under the updated guidance, using non-cash public benefits like Medicaid or SNAP will not, by itself, disqualify an applicant. A new version of the I-four eighty-five form is also now required for these applications.

And finally, Markets.

It was a positive day for the major indices. The Nasdaq Composite had the strongest showing, rising about one-point-seven percent. The S and P 500 gained a little over one percent, and the Dow added about zero-point-six percent.

Looking at your watchlist, the big tech names were all in the green. Nvidia led the pack, jumping about two-and-a-half percent. Amazon also had a strong session, rising just over two percent, while Microsoft, Apple, and Alphabet all posted gains of more than one percent.

That's your briefing. Have a great day.
